title: Microstructure-Dependent surface degradation under deuterium plasma Exposure: A comparative study of DS-W, APS-W, and PW
abstract: Tungsten (W) is a leading plasma-facing material for fusion reactors, while its performance is strongly governed by microstructure-dependent deformation and hydrogen isotope retention. This study aimed to establish a clear relationship between microstructure, mechanical properties, and deuterium (D) plasma-induced surface degradation in tungsten materials. A systematic comparative investigation was conducted on detonation-sprayed tungsten (DS-W), atmospheric plasma-sprayed tungsten (APS-W), and pure tungsten (PW) for the first time. The samples were exposed to D plasma with an incident kinetic energy of 40 eV at different exposure temperatures (500, 650, and 800 K) under constant fluence (1 × 10 25 D/m 2 ) and different exposure fluences (1 × 10 24 , 5 × 10 24 , and 1 × 10 25 D/m 2 ) under constant temperature (650 K). Microstructural characterization, surface morphology analysis, and thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) were employed to evaluate deformation behavior, damage evolution, and D retention. The results showed that DS-W exhibited the highest pre-exposure hardness due to its fine-grained and dense structure, while APS-W exhibited the lowest pre-exposure hardness and more severe surface degradation because of its porous nature. PW exhibited the least surface damage under plasma exposure, whereas DS-W showed more uniform and controlled damage than APS-W. D retention is highest in APS-W, followed by DS-W and PW. Overall, the study highlighted the important key role of microstructure in governing plasma-induced damage and provides useful insights for improving tungsten-based materials for fusion applications.

title: Feasibility study of deuterium recombination front measurement by analyzing Zeeman effect on chord-integrated Ar I line spectra at 912 and 965 nm in JT-60SA
abstract: In this study, we evaluate a diagnostic method to estimate the deuterium recombination front position in detached plasmas by analyzing the Zeeman effect on near-infrared Ar I lines. Using SONIC simulation data for a JT-60SA detached divertor plasma and collisional-radiative models, we analyze chord-integrated Ar I line spectra at 912 n m ( 4 s 3 / 2 2 - 4 p 1 / 2 1 ) and 965 n m ( 4 s 3 / 2 1 - 4 p 1 / 2 1 ). The recombination front and the Ar I line emissivity peak are located within a distance of 3.6 mm. At the recombination front position, the total line width of the Ar I lines is about half of their Zeeman splitting. The analysis of the Zeeman effect on the chord-integrated spectra reveals that the emission positions estimated from the Ar I lines at 912 and 965 nm are at a distance of 1.80 and 2.39 cm from the actual recombination front toward the upstream direction, respectively. These results demonstrate that the recombination front position can be estimated.

title: Energy balance and surface diagnostics of runaway electron beam termination in the TCV tokamak
abstract: The energy balance of the final collapse of runaway electron (RE) beams in TCV is quantified by combining calorimetry, infrared thermography, bolometry, magnetic reconstructions and Monte Carlo simulations. The balance accounts for the redistribution of the stored kinetic and magnetic energy into plasma-facing components, radiation and inductive coupling to the vessel. For plasma currents of I p ∼ 150 kA , the RE kinetic energy obtained from the balance is 15 to 20 kJ, comparable to the poloidal magnetic energy stored inside the vessel. Discharges are performed in the benign termination scenario with different degrees of mitigation. Where mitigation is incomplete, 55 to 65% of the stored energy is deposited on the central column graphite tiles, 20 to 30% is radiated and about 15% is coupled to the vessel. In the mitigated case the radiated fraction increases and the deposited fraction decreases, showing that effective mitigation spreads the energy over a larger area of plasma-facing components. Calorimetry and infrared thermography show that the deposition is close to toroidally symmetric. GEANT4 simulations at the grazing incidence of the field lines on the central column give deposition profiles that are maximal at the surface for all energies and pitch angles considered. They also show that photon escape is a minor fraction of the energy budget. A one-dimensional thermal model driven by these profiles and by the calorimetric energy reproduces the infrared surface temperature evolution for electron energies of 2 to 5 MeV, depending on the pitch angle, below the upper bound of the average energy derived from the balance. These results provide an experimental benchmark for RE energy deposition. Low-current devices constrain the magnetic-to-kinetic energy conversion that dominates mitigation in ITER only indirectly.

title: Analysis of solid boron injection for ITER
abstract: Since ITER will now operate with a full tungsten divertor and first wall (Loarte et al. 2025), the ITER Organization is considering boron wall conditioning schemes to getter oxygen and reduce tungsten sputtering to avoid excessive radiation to ensure that ITER can reach and sustain high- performance plasma operation. ITER has adopted Glow Discharge Boronization (GDB) (Wauters et al. 2025) in deuterated diborane (B 2 D 6 ) as its main technique, which can only be performed in the absence of magnetic fields, but has also requested a study to determine how effective solid boron injection (SBI), which can be performed during plasma operation, using either an Impurity Powder Dropper (IPD) (Nagy et al. 2018) or a boron pellet injector (Snipes et al. 2024), might be as a risk mitigation to achieving Q=10. Solid impurity injection has been used for decades as a wall conditioning technique on numerous tokamaks and stellarators around the world (Snipes et al. 1992; Vorenkamp et al. 2017; Bortolon et al., 2019, 2020; Xu et al. 2023; Gilson et al. 2021; Lunsford et al. 2022; Effenberg et al. 2022; Bodner et al. 2022). The study presented here begins to assess SBI on ITER by first quantifying the boron source term across a particle size scan from 1 μ m to 5 mm diameter and an injection velocity scan from 5 – 200 m/s for several ITER plasma conditions: (1) Start of Research Operations (SRO) diverted L-mode, (2) Q = 10 H-mode, and (3) low plasma current and low power limiter operation. Modeling of the ablation, transport, erosion and redeposition of solid boron is being carried out with the Dust Injection Simulator (DIS) (Nespoli et al. 2021), the Neutral Gas Shielding (NGS) (Parks et al., 1988; Parks et al., 1994; Lunsford, et al. 2017), EMC3-EIRENE (Feng et al. 2014; Effenberg et al. 2021) and WallDYN3D (Schmid, 2020) models. In the first steps presented here, the DIS and NGS models are compared for calculating the boron source term that is then used as input to EMC3-EIRENE and will later be used with WallDYN3D.

title: Reliability-Based Optimization of Concrete Gamma-Ray Shielding Thickness: A Methodological Framework for 137Cs Sources
abstract: Reliable gamma-ray shielding design requires balancing radiological protection and construction costs while accounting for uncertainties in source characteristics, material properties, and geometry. This study presents a reliability-based optimization framework for determining the optimum thickness of homogeneous concrete shielding against gamma radiation from a hypothetical 137 Cs point source. The dose-response model combines exponential attenuation with the ANSI/ANS-6.4.3 geometric-progression (GP) buildup formulation. Uncertainties in source activity, gamma-dose constant, concrete density, shielding thickness, and source-to-receptor distances are incorporated into a probabilistic limit-state function. Dose-limit exceedance probabilities are evaluated using the First-Order Reliability Method (FORM), Monte Carlo Simulation (MCS), and Weighted Average Simulation Method (WASM). Life-cycle cost optimization is performed using the Golden Section Search (GSS) and compared with the Firefly Algorithm (FA). A comprehensive parametric investigation examines the effects of benchmark reliability levels, receptor distance, annual release probability, service life, discount rate, and economic consequence ratio. Experimental comparisons with published 137 Cs transmission measurements indicate conservative GP predictions under normal incidence, while revealing limitations associated with oblique irradiation. The numerical methods show close agreement, with FORM providing substantial computational advantages. Optimum shielding thickness is governed primarily by reliability requirements and receptor distance, whereas economic parameters become more influential at lower reliability levels. A database comprising 116,640 optimum solutions supports reliability-based design charts and sensitivity analyses. The proposed framework provides a practical basis for preliminary shielding optimization, although its quantitative predictions remain dependent on the adopted source geometry and attenuation assumptions.

title: Long-term high-sensitivity operation of a reprogrammable floating-gate MOS dosimeter: Gamma irradiation and a non-ionizing UV control
abstract: Commercial electrically programmable analog devices (EPADs) based on a reprogrammable floating-gate MOS structure were operated in a high-sensitivity ( HighSens ) regime, in which two devices on the same ALD1108E chip alternate between radiation monitoring and electrical recharging of the floating gate. Long-term experiments were performed under 6 0 ⁢ C o gamma irradiation and under 311 nm UV exposure using matched cycling and reprogramming protocols. Under zero-bias gamma irradiation, HighSens operation provided a near-linear reconstructed dose response with a sensitivity of 8 . 9 5 m V / G y up to 560 Gy, without functional failure. Static positive bias and negative bias produced a progressive loss of reprogramming efficiency and eventual failure to restore the target threshold voltage. A matched zero-bias UV control, in which 311 nm photons discharge the floating gate without generating electron–hole pairs in S i O 2 , showed stable reprogramming jumps and no device failure over a larger equivalent-dose range. The comparison indicates that the long-term degradation of reprogramming efficiency under gamma irradiation is associated with ionizing-radiation effects in combination with repeated electrical stress, rather than with electrical stress alone.

title: Enhancing the nuclear safety regulatory framework and technical standards for maritime non-light-water SMRs
abstract: The 2023 net-zero-by-2050 greenhouse-gas strategy of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has renewed interest in nuclear propulsion at sea, and Korea is advancing non-light-water small modular reactors (SMRs) for ship propulsion and floating power generation. Korea’s Nuclear Safety Act, however, licenses only light- and heavy-water reactors on fixed land sites. This study surveys marine nuclear regulation in ten nations, keeping only issues common to five or more and beyond unilateral competence, and tests the Nuclear Safety Act against the Ship Safety Act. Seven such issues are identified: the 1981 IMO Code’s pressurized-water-reactor premise; the lack of legal status for non-self-propelled floating plants; the undefined nuclear–maritime division of jurisdiction; exclusion of ship-installed reactors from civil-liability regimes; port entry approval; dual licensing; and the demonstration–regulation vicious cycle. Revision of the IMO Code, targeted for 2030, is the global critical path. Fourteen further issues are traced through the marine-specific life-cycle stages—siting and installation, operation, maintenance, decommissioning—each remedy assigned to a named instrument. A three-part test for the limits of delegated legislation shows that seven of the remedies proposed—six of the fourteen, together with the allocation of ministerial jurisdiction—require prior amendment of the parent statute, fixing the order of reform.

title: Comparison of 1-D and 3-D simulations and parametric study of a steady state natural circulation loop with internal heat generating fluid
abstract: In liquid-fueled molten salt reactors (MSRs), decay heat is generated volumetrically within the fuel salt and is distributed throughout the circulation loop following reactor shutdown. This internal heat generation (IHG) can alter the buoyancy distribution and heat removal characteristics of the natural circulation loop (NCL), resulting in significantly different behavior compared to that observed in a conventional NCL with a localized heater. In this study, a geometry-dependent 1-D steady-state model was developed for an NCL with IHG. To assess the applicability and limitations of the proposed 1-D model, 3-D CFD simulations were performed over laminar to turbulent flow regimes. The 1-D model predicted the steady-state Reynolds number ( Re ss ) within a 7% difference from the CFD results in the turbulent regime, whereas relatively larger discrepancies were observed in the laminar and transitional regimes. Detailed CFD analysis showed that IHG induced local buoyancy effects and increased the overall flow resistance, causing the 1-D model to overpredict the Re ss in the laminar regime. This overprediction may lead to an underestimation of the maximum fluid temperature, resulting in non-conservative thermal predictions for MSR passive heat removal systems. Based on this assessment, reactor-scale IHG-NCL analyses were conducted using the 1-D model only in the turbulent regime, by varying the cooler length and cooler position. These findings clarify the range of applicability of the 1-D model assumptions in IHG-NCL modeling and provide guidance for cooler geometry design in MSR applications.

title: Multiphysics tritium transport modelling of the ARC breeding blanket with FESTIM
abstract: Accurate prediction of tritium behaviour in molten salt breeding blankets is essential for the design and safe operation of ARC-class fusion reactors. This work presents a fully open-source, component-scale multiphysics framework for modelling tritium transport in an ARC liquid immersion blanket. Neutron transport, thermal hydraulics, and hydrogen isotope transport are coupled using OpenMC, OpenFOAM, and FESTIM, leveraging dedicated tools enabling direct transfer of spatially resolved fields between solvers. Assuming a zero inlet concentration and a fusion power of 525 MW, steady-state simulations predict a total tritium inventory of approximately 243 mg in the liquid breeder, corresponding to a mean residence time of approximately 4 min, with the blanket reaching steady-state tritium throughput within approximately 30 min, which is of a similar order to previous system-level estimates. The results show that tritium transport is dominated by turbulence-enhanced diffusion, with strong localisation in flow stagnation regions and reduced accumulation in highly turbulent zones. Sensitivity analyses indicate that predicted inventories are governed primarily by the numerical stabilisation scheme, with only a modest dependence on the turbulent Schmidt number. The proposed workflow provides a transparent and extensible basis for high-fidelity analysis of tritium transport in ARC-class breeding blankets.

title: A magnetostatic shield for the RF driver: impact on the plasma properties & extraction performance of the ITER Negative IonSource
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The experimental fusion reactor ITER relies on neutral beam injectors as auxiliary heating system, providing 33 MW of heating power to the fusion plasma.  ITER neutral beams are obtained through neutralisation of negative ion hydrogen/deuterium beams accelerated up to 1 MeV. The ion source consists of an inductively coupled plasma powered by radio-frequency (RF) generators, where a magnetic filter field is necessary to lower electron temperature and density in the extraction region, minimizing the destruction of negative ions. However, an excessive filter field in the driver region was found to limit the RF coupling, motivating the investigation of a magnetostatic shield placed around the RF drivers to screen stray magnetic fields and reduce the filter field effect on the driver plasma, without compromising electron filtering in the extraction region.This work presents a plasma characterization study of the magnetostatic shield effect, tested at SPIDER and MINION, two test facilities hosted at Consorzio RFX in Padova (Italy) within the Neutral Beam Test Facility (NBTF). Results from SPIDER are discussed, focusing on plasma properties measured with Langmuir probes and optical emission spectroscopy, supported by a Collisional Radiative (CR) model. It is shown that the extracted negative ion current density is nearly unaffected by the shield, even at high filter field values, while a wider range of plasma grid currents becomes accessible without left-right asymmetry in the RF driver pairs.</jats:p>

title: Towards development and validation of an integrated SOLPS-EPED model in MAST-U
abstract: We present and partially validate an extended coupling workflow linking the edge physics of SOLPS-ITER scrape-off layer simulations to EPED pedestal predictions in MAST-U. The workflow uses a recently extended heuristic density model to map separatrix conditions to pedestal top densities: an advancement beyond the empirical trends used in previous coupling demonstrations. The new coupling is tested against MAST-U experiments in which we aim to change the divertor neutral source fueling the pedestal top. Experimental trends in pedestal performance are qualitatively well-reproduced by SOLPS-EPED when implementing geometry changes to the divertor closure, and the coupling methodology provides a good model-to-model quantitative consistency to standalone EPED modeling. Analysis of the neutral sourcing in SOLPS identifies that closure changes are not the dominant source in an observed 30% increase in neutral density with an open divertor configuration; rather, changes to the high-field side fueling efficiency likely dominate over divertor sources. Changes to the divertor pressure at fixed geometry through divertor gas puffing result in a degradation in pedestal performance that cannot be captured at present by the SOLPS-EPED coupling. Challenges in disentangling divertor physics from the high-field side fueling and identifying missing pedestal physics beyond the EPED assumptions are discussed towards improving the modular coupling in future work at MAST-U.

title: How E×B drifts impact the redistribution of trace densities in an island divertor
abstract: In island-diverted stellarators, the impurity physics in the edge magnetic islands requires a detailed understanding of the flux-surface perpendicular transport processes. Recent developments in the Hermes-family of edge fluid transport simulations enable the investigation of drift effects in stellarators. We use the drift-implementation to investigate the transport of a trace species in a simplified island divertor geometry and compare purely diffusive perpendicular and parallel transport to additionally drift-driven dynamics. When seeding the trace species in just one island, diffusive transport leads to fluxes in the adjacent islands and the confined region, whereas the E × B drift leads to transport in one preferential direction. Drifts require a few milliseconds to redistribute the trace species, while diffusive transport requires more than one order of magnitude longer. We demonstrate that transport of trace species into the confined region is reduced by the E × B drift. The gradient-driven nature of the diffusive flux leads to strong gradients between islands, which are not present in the drift-driven case and the E × B drift significantly reduces the asymmetries between the islands.

title: Grain boundary mediated resistance to helium bubble induced mechanical degradation in CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy
abstract: Mechanical degradation driven by helium bubbles is a well-known concern in nuclear structural materials, yet how microstructural architecture controls this behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) remains an open question. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out on CoCrCuFeNi HEA to compare single-crystal and polycrystalline responses under systematically varied He bubble conditions. Under the conditions of the present simulations, microstructural type proved far more consequential than bubble presence, number, or location. The single-crystal model suffered a 79.0 % drop in ultimate tensile strength at 300 K upon bubble introduction, whereas the polycrystalline model lost only 3.6 % − a disparity traced to grain-boundary suppression of sessile dislocation lock formation and broader redistribution of plastic strain. Despite producing nearly identical macroscopic stress–strain curves, grain-interior (GI) and grain-boundary (GB) bubble configurations follow divergent microstructural paths: GB bubbles accommodate deformation through greater volumetric expansion, while GI bubbles preferentially trigger hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure formation consistent with stacking faults along {111} planes, with the dominant mechanism shifting at roughly 6–8 % strain. Within the limited range of grain sizes examined, d ≈ 12.4 nm offered the most stable post-peak behavior, balancing grain boundary density against intragranular dislocation storage. While these results are limited to the present simulation conditions, they point to grain boundary density as a key microstructural parameter governing resistance to helium-bubble-induced mechanical degradation, motivating future experimental and multiscale modeling efforts.
title_ko: CoCrCuFeNi 고엔트로피 합금에서 헬륨 기포 유도 기계적 열화에 대한 결정립계 매개 저항

title: First-principles prediction of solute segregation in dilute iron transition-metal alloys under strain: Significance of elastic modulus mismatch
abstract: Current theories on irradiation induced segregation of solutes, including the solute-point defect coupling diffusion model and the size mismatch-driven mechanism, may not fully explain the experimental segregation and precipitation phenomena of Ni and Si in dilute iron alloys under irradiation. This work presents three expressions for segregation energy under hydrostatic volumetric, orthorhombic, and monoclinic strains, which enable the calculation of segregation energy of a solute in body-centered cubic Fe solvent under a strain from the concentration and size mismatch of the solute, and the elastic modulus mismatch of the alloy. These expressions are valid for random solid solutions under moderate strain. To facilitate such predictions, we calculated the size factor Ω s f for solutes, bulk modulus factor B m f , tetragonal shear modulus factor C ′ m f and single-crystal shear modulus factor C 44 m f for iron transition-metal alloys at concentrations from 0.4 to 2.08 at.% based on density-functional theory simulations. The segregation energies ( E s e g ) of solute Ni ( 1.85 at.%) and Si ( 0.4 at.%) under diluted and compressive volumetric strains with a magnitude of 0.06 were predicted to be - 0.337 and - 0.103 eV, respectively, suggesting that driven by size mismatch and bulk modulus mismatch, these two solutes have a very high tendency of segregation. The predicted E s e g of Ni ( 1.85 at.%) and Si ( 0.4 at.%) are - 0.0246 and - 0.0773 eV, respectively, under the orthorhombic strain of 0.06, indicating that they are both highly inclined to segregate driven by tetragonal shear modulus mismatch. A detailed discussion was presented on the correlations between these elastic modulus factors and differential charge density on the surfaces of Wigner-Seitz cells enclosing the solutes.

title: The science of compressional heating on the LM26 magnetized target fusion experiment
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Lawson Machine 26 (LM26) operating at General Fusion has demonstrated compressional heating of a spherical tokamak deuterium plasma as it was compressed by an imploding solid lithium liner.  Results from the first 11 compression experiments on LM26 are presented, the highest-performing of which show more than a three-fold increase in electron temperature, a ten-fold increase in density, and a ten-fold increase in poloidal field in the plasma driven by three-fold radial compression.   &#xD;The experimental device and its instrumentation are reviewed in detail, followed by direct observations from each of the key diagnostics for liner trajectory and plasma properties, measuring increases in magnetic field, electron density, as well as emission of neutrons, X-rays, and visible radiation. &#xD;Observations from fast-camera images during compression provide detailed context for interpreting the spatial structure of plasma-wall interaction. &#xD;Overviews of the various models developed and used in the analysis are presented.  Diagnostic data are used to reconstruct the experimental equilibrium state in computational modeling as a function of time.  &#xD;The results indicate the reconstructions are sufficiently accurate to match the essential observations from the experiment, validating the models and building confidence in the stability and transport analyses that support the key conclusions.  &#xD;Trends across the full set of 11 compression shots are presented, and a more detailed examination of the high-performance shots are given individually.  &#xD;The key conclusions of the integrated physics model specifically indicate that compressional heating was achieved in this set of experiments, as evidenced by the balance of heating power from compression, Ohmic heating from plasma current, and losses to the boundary necessary to match the experimental data. &#xD;A majority of the increase in temperature is attributable to compressional heating.  &#xD;An increase in neutron flux is also observed during compression. The results provide a basis for planned improvements to the LM26 facility that will enable the compression of magnetized plasma to increasingly higher densities and temperatures.</jats:p>

title: Nonlinear modeling of Edge Localized Modes control using Resonant Magnetic Perturbation on HL-3
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Utilizing the three-dimensional nonlinear code JOREK, the dynamics of edge localized modes (ELMs) evolution with the application of resonant magnetic perturbation (RMP) have been modeled for the HL-3 tokamak. Scanning of the RMP coil current shows that, with increasing of the RMP coil current, ELMs are first mitigated followed by total suppression. Calculation of the time correlation function, as well as the Poisson bracket quantity, indicates a significant energy transfer between toroidal modes, implying that application of the RMP field acts as a constant external drive which greatly facilitates the energy redistribution between toroidal modes through nonlinear mode coupling. For the ELM mitigation case, a single most unstable mode is replaced with several unstable modes at similar amplitudes due to energy redistribution, and large ELMs are replaced with more frequent but small-sized bursts. When the RMP field is sufficiently strong, a substantial edge transport is induced to reduce the height of the edge pedestal and bring the pressure gradient to a value below the stability boundary of the peeling-ballooning modes, thus fully suppresses the onset of ELM bursts. Mode braking of the edge instability has been found with application of the RMP field. The static RMP mode dominates at the high field side of the torus, while slowly rotating toroidal modes still exist at the low field side.</jats:p>

title: Nonlinear evolution of perturbatively driven kinetic instabilities far from marginal stability
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Kinetic instabilities develop when a system's distribution function deviates from thermal equilibrium in such a way that allows free energy from that distribution to drive resonant modes. Motivated by the case of Alfv'enic instabilities driven by minority populations of energetic particles in tokamak plasmas, we consider a kinetic instability with perturbative drive far from its instability threshold, where a theoretical description of the time evolution has not yet been established. In cases with steady-state saturation levels, we find that the mode first evolves linearly, driven by the positive distribution gradient, then undergoes a fast, strongly nonlinear transition where the distribution function slope is completely flattened around the resonance. The system then evolves in a nonlinear regime driven by the balance of the wave drive and dissipation until reaching saturation. The strongly nonlinear transition is sufficiently fast that it can be treated as occurring instantaneously, and by considering a time-local approximation for the distribution after the flattening has occurred, we find a closed-form analytical solution for the mode amplitude in the nonlinear phase.  A compact continuous solution for the entire time evolution of the mode amplitude is therefore constructed, and this result is shown to agree closely with nonlinear kinetic simulations.</jats:p>

title: Design and modeling of a Runaway Electron Mitigation Coil for the TCV Tokamak
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A novel Runaway Electron Mitigation Coil (REMC) has been designed for the Tokamak à Configuration Variable (TCV) to enable the passive deconfinement of relativistic runaway electrons (REs). This non-axisymmetric coil is designed to couple passively to the disruption-induced loop voltage during the current quench phase, generating strong non-axisymmetric fields to destroy magnetic flux surfaces and drive beneficial MHD. The TCV REMC is designed to drive an $n=1$ perturbation while maximizing inductive coupling to the plasma, thereby inducing significant current in the coil. It represents the first passively driven coil of its kind to be implemented in a plasma with an RE plateau, thereby enabling a direct test of its ability to prevent RE beam formation. The ThinCurr electromagnetic modeling code was used to explore various coil configurations under realistic machine constraints. This model incorporates a detailed representation of the vacuum vessel, including material thicknesses and resistivities, and enables the evaluation of both induced coil currents and the resulting 3D magnetic field structures. The results highlight the importance of capturing the physics of the currents induced in the wall and therefore support the use of ThinCurr as the primary development tool. Based on these vacuum criteria, the three most promising coil configurations were selected. At the expected coil resistance of $200~\mu\Omega$, the configuration selected for initial installation is predicted to produce a maximum coil current of $13.3$ kA and an $n=1$ poloidal field exceeding $0.5\%$ of the background toroidal field by the end of the current quench. The REMC will be validated by assessing its ability to couple to the plasma current, influence the current quench rate, and prevent RE plateau formation. Beyond TCV, the results of this study provide valuable insights for future tokamaks considering similar passive coils, such as SPARC and STEP, and contribute to evaluating the potential role of passive mitigation systems in reactor-scale devices.</jats:p>

title: Robust Identification of Unseen Radionuclide Mixtures Using Compact Structured Representations
abstract: Identifying previously unseen combinations of known radionuclides in low-resolution gamma-ray spectrometry remains challenging under spectral degradation and varying acquisition conditions. This study evaluates three multi-label architectures—1D-CNN, AE+MLP, and Hilbert-AE+MLP—for radionuclide-mixture identification under controlled spectral perturbations and domain shifts. A dataset of 4,158 MCNP6-simulated spectra, covering six radionuclides and all 63 non-empty compositions, was generated using a 2″ × 2″ NaI(Tl) detector model. Composition-level partitioning and six-fold cross-validation were used to assess generalization to previously unseen compositions. Under ideal conditions, the F1-scores were 0.984 ± 0.033, 0.998 ± 0.005, and 0.997 ± 0.006 for 1D-CNN, AE+MLP, and Hilbert-AE+MLP, respectively. Under spectral perturbations, Hilbert-AE+MLP showed consistent performance across the tested gain-displacement and resolution-degradation conditions, achieving an F1-score of 0.889 ± 0.003 under 12.0% resolution degradation and ±15% gain displacement without retraining. On strictly unseen experimental compositions, it achieved precision, recall, and F1-score of 1.00, while its mean per-isotope F1-score on strictly unseen short-time compositions was 0.690 ± 0.009. Controlled comparisons and locality analysis indicate that the observed robustness is associated with structured preservation of local spectral neighborhoods in the Hilbert representation.

title: Optimization of the retrieval-augmented generation workflow for question answering on nuclear safety regulations
abstract: The baseline retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow often fails to meet the specific needs of high-stakes domains such as question answering (Q&A) for nuclear safety regulations. To improve answer accuracy, multiple strategies have been adopted to optimize the retrieval, query and generation stages of the RAG workflow. The Q&A performance under different single-stage, dual-stage, and three-stage RAG optimization strategies have been compared. The Q&A performance under all 2048 possible RAG workflow configurations has been exhaustively evaluated, and the top-ranked workflows have been tested on self-constructed QA datasets. The results indicate that the RAG-based Q&A system significantly outperforms general large language models (LLMs), and the three-stage optimized RAG workflow achieves substantially higher answer accuracy than the baseline.

title: Numerical research on response of fluid-induced vibration of reactor core barrel
abstract: : The flow-induced vibration analysis of the reactor core barrel is very important for the safe operation of the reactor. Based on the theory of power spectral density (PSD) analysis for random vibration and the previous research on hydrodynamic loads on the surface of core barrel, a set of analytical method for calculating the flow-induced vibration response of core barrel of the pressurized water reactor is proposed in this paper. Firstly, the finite element model (FEM) of core barrel was established, including the setting of appropriate constraint conditions and the calculation of the additional mass of the structure in water. Secondly, the correlation length of core barrel was calculated based on the load data. And the load spectrum on the surface of core barrel was constructed according to our previous research. Thirdly, based on the ANSYS Program, the PSD spectrum analysis of random vibration under multiple groups of dense frequencies was completed respectively. Finally, the combination of Square Root of the Sum of the Squares (SRSS) about the spectrum analysis results of each group was carried out. To verify the analytical method, a flow-induced vibration response test of the reactor core barrel was conducted. According to research, the theoretical results are approximately 40% higher than the experimental measurements. The sensitivity analysis of the correlation length indicates that the magnitude of flow-induced vibration response is directly proportional to the magnitude of the correlation length.

title: Joint optimization of analysis-unit selection and scored cell number for AI-assisted dicentric chromosome biodosimetry
abstract: Background Rapid biological dose assessment is essential for radiation emergency response, but AI-assisted dicentric chromosome analysis requires explicit selection of valid analysis units and determination of a scored cell number. Their interdependence remains unclear. Methods Dicentric chromosome assay data obtained under acute whole-body gamma-ray exposure conditions were evaluated using retention criteria based on the mode ± K median absolute deviations of the chromosome-count distribution (K = 2–9). At each criterion, 1,000 bootstrap iterations quantified dose variability. The required scored cell number was defined as the earliest point at which agreement in the coefficient of variation was sustained at ≥ 97 %. Results Dose variability decreased as the scored cell number increased, with diminishing gains from additional scoring. K = 2 retained 64.5 % of analysis units, whereas newly included units decreased from 6.4 % at K = 3 to 1.3 % at K = 9. Broadening the retention criterion minimally changed the required scored cell number or estimated dose but generally widened the 95 % confidence interval. Conclusion Joint optimization of analysis-unit selection and scored cell number provides a basis for balancing scoring efficiency and analytical burden against dose-estimation uncertainty, supporting resource-efficient biological dosimetry during large-scale radiation emergency response.

title: Interpretable machine learning-aided mix design of uranium tailings-based geopolymers: strength, microstructure and radon exhalation
abstract: : Mix design of alkali-activated uranium tailings-based geopolymers still relies on trial and error, hindering low-carbon solidification of radioactive tailings. Here, geopolymer monoliths were fabricated from uranium tailings, ground granulated blast-furnace slag, silica fume and fly ash, and assessed through single-factor and L16(4 5 ) orthogonal experiments, XRD, FTIR, SEM-EDS, closed-chamber radon measurement and explainable machine learning. A dense amorphous C-(A)-S-H/zeolitic gel formed and acted as the primary binder; the maximum 28-day unconfined compressive strength reached 29.01 MPa. Radon exhalation fell by 96.6–99.4% relative to raw tailings, keeping every mix 14–79 times below the EJ/T 977-95 screening limit. XGBoost outperformed four benchmark models under repeated cross-validation (holdout R 2 = 0.923), and SHAP analysis recovered a factor hierarchy consistent with orthogonal range analysis and microstructural evidence. Surrogate optimization and design of experiments converged on one recipe (activator modulus 1.4, liquid–solid ratio 0.20, alkali equivalent 12%, modified material dosage 15%); a confirmatory cast validated this recommendation, its 28-day strength falling within the bootstrap prediction interval and its radon exhalation the lowest of all mixes. This workflow provides a low-carbon, interpretable route to intelligent mix design for radioactive-waste solidification.

title: Application of cosine similarity analysis for monitoring the recovery of mobile inspection radiation sources
abstract: In mobile radiation monitoring equipment, there is a risk of loss of radiation source during transport and field work. In order to mitigate the risk of loss of radiation source in mobile radiographic operation, this study proposes a dynamic monitoring approach based on Cosine Similarity Analysis for real-time tracking the location of radioactive sources during recovery process. In this method, real-time radiation dose rate data is continuously collected throughout the source deployment and recovery phases using a mobile radiographic system. Measured point - Dose rate distribution curves are then constructed and cosine similarity algorithms are employed to quantify the spatial distribution consistency between the deployment and recovery dose rate profiles. Experimental validation was conducted under normal recovery conditions as well as three Source-Drop scenarios occurring at the container exit, along the transfer path and at the inspection site. By employing a Sliding-Window algorithm to dynamically compute cosine similarity, the proposed method enables real-time detection of significant decreases in similarity, thereby achieving precise identification of source drop location. In addition, robustness analysis was performed to establish a three-level risk criterion for classifying operational risk. Through a combined analysis of data obtained during the deployment and recovery phases, the proposed method provides a highly responsive and accurate intelligent early-warning mechanism for monitoring the status of mobile radiographic sources. The method effectively reduces the probability of source loss in field operations and enhances the efficiency of source retrieval, demonstrating substantial potential for engineering applications in radiation safety management.

title: Euler–Euler simulation of flow-induced vibrations of an obstacle in two-phase pipe flow
abstract: Understanding Flow-Induced Vibrations (FIV) is essential for ensuring the safety of steam generators in nuclear power plants. Unchecked vibrations can cause tube wear, fatigue or even failure, posing potential safety risks. In U-tube configurations where two-phase cross-flow is prevalent, these issues become more severe. While this phenomenon has been thoroughly examined in single-phase cross-flow, its behavior in two-phase flows is less understood. The Horizon Europe project GO-VIKING aims to tackle these issues by utilizing experimental setups to investigate two-phase flow-induced vibrations. These facilities emphasize the Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) between tube bundles and air–water cross-flows. This paper presents both classical and hybrid Euler–Euler simulations of FIV of a cylindrical obstacle in two-phase pipe flow, as recently experimentally studied in the PILULE experiment performed by Electricité de France R&D. The emphasis of this work lies on the assessment of the two-phase modeling methodology itself, with the flow-induced vibration of the obstacle serving as an application and validation case. The LogMoM model is used for the poly-disperse bubble distribution, including advanced closure models for coalescence and break-up. Particularly in the wake of the obstacle, coalescence and break-up play an important role in the redistribution of void. In turn, drag and lift forces acting on the obstacle are predicted. The presented work contributes to establishing a validated two-phase flow FSI simulation strategy of FIV in cross-flows over tube bundles. The paper demonstrates the shortcomings of both the classical model, which fails to capture large bubbles and pressure fluctuations, and the hybrid model, which is seen to produce fluctuations but is too aggressive in its transition to resolved bubbles. This shows that further developments are needed in terms of pressure fluctuation modeling as well as fundamental hybrid model improvements.

title: Development of surrogate model for reactor cooling system based on ASTEC simulations during the early phase of station blackout
abstract: In this work, metamodels capable of reproducing the thermal-hydraulic behavior of subsystems of the reactor coolant system (RCS) during the early phase of a Station Blackout (SBO) leading to a severe accident—i.e., up to the point of fission product release in the RCS—are proposed as a first step toward the development of accelerated surrogate models for severe accident simulations. The work is performed in the frame of the EU-funded project ASSAS, which aims at developing a basic-principles severe accident simulator for a generic 1300 MW pressurized water reactor (PWR), by replacing ASTEC (severe accident code developed by ASNR) models with Machine Learning (ML) surrogate models. The work presented here focuses on the thermal-hydraulic CESAR module for the primary and secondary circuits. A suitable training dataset must be generated. A base case scenario is considered, involving an SBO without any safety measures until the onset of fission product release. From this base case, various calculations are performed by depressurizing remotely the primary circuit at different times, followed by the recovery of emergency water injection, also at different times. From these ASTEC calculations only the variables needed for the surrogate model development are extracted. These include state variables for each control volume within the RCS domain, boundary conditions, and additional variables that may provide information about the overall evolution of the accident and could be useful for ML. The surrogate models are expected to compute each time step while also accounting for user decisions interactively during the accident simulation. The ML method considered here is based on Recurrent Neural Networks, which are commonly used for time series. The developed LSTM-based surrogate models achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) on the order of 10 −3 on an independent test dataset. Temperatures and steam pressures were predicted with the highest accuracy, whereas void fractions and hydrogen partial pressures exhibited larger errors. Among the four metamodels, the steam generator secondary side showed the most robust predictive performance, while the primary side was more sensitive to rare events. Larger error metrics were especially found during changes in operational state.

title: Water Distillation for Light/Heavy Water Detritiation and Heavy Water Upgrading
abstract: Water distillation is a mature, simple, and reliable separation technology that is uniquely well suited to address water isotope enrichment/separation encountered in light water– or heavy water–based fission nuclear reactors and fusion fuel cycles. It can be used for light water detritiation, heavy water upgrading, and heavy water detritiation. Although the elementary separation factors of the H/T, H/D, D/T, and 16O/18O isotope pairs are small (1.005 to 1.20 over the 5°C to 70°C operating range), modern advanced water distillation packings (with significantly smaller height equivalent to a theoretical plate) have reduced the required column height by a factor of 3 to 4 relative to conventional CY-type packing, making large-scale implementation increasingly attractive.This article presents a unified approach to three representative cases, using one multicomponent model that tracks all 18 hydrogen and oxygen isotopologues of water: (i) steady-state light water detritiation, (ii) heavy water upgrading combined with detritiation of the light water head product, including a CANDU® 6 primary heat transport (PHT) case in which a small auxiliary column also removes tritium from the upgraded heavy water, and (iii) deep detritiation of a heavy water inventory by Rayleigh batch distillation.The MESH (material balance, equilibrium, summation, enthalpy) equations, the vapor pressure isotope effects, the Rayleigh equation, and a lumped tritium balance for the CANDU moderator and PHT systems are presented in a single consistent notation. The simulations, which predict a detritiation factor (DF) of ≈104 at 25 kg/h for light water detritiation in a 550-stage column, show that, with an enrichment factor of 400 (≈650 theoretical stages at a D2O/DTO separation factor of 1.014), Rayleigh batch distillation can reduce the tritium activity of heavy water from 1 Ci/kg to the virgin D2O level (≈1.3 µCi/kg) while withdrawing only ≈3.3% of the inventory as a ≈30 Ci/kg concentrate at the cost of a large boilup.The analysis shows that the predicted DFs are governed mainly by the separation factors and the number of theoretical stages. Combined steady-state and batch (Rayleigh) operation, therefore, provides a complete toolkit for water isotope management in tritium facilities such as CANDU reactors and ITER.

title: Ultrasonic Multipoint Waveguide Temperature Sensor for Divertor Diagnostics in Fusion Power Plants
abstract: An ultrasonic multipoint waveguide temperature sensor (UMWTS) has been developed as a laboratory proof of concept for multipoint temperature monitoring through a single compact metallic waveguide. Periodic notches machined into the waveguide form acoustic Bragg gratings, which act as frequency-selective reflectors. Different notch spacings allow for the gratings to be designed with distinct reflection frequencies. Temperature-dependent changes in the elastic properties, material density, and grating pitch produce measurable frequency shifts in the reflected ultrasonic signals.Ultrasonic guided waves are launched and received using a transducer driven by short electrical pulses or tone bursts. Two stainless steel waveguides, one containing five uniform-frequency gratings and the other containing five multifrequency gratings, were fabricated and tested using laboratory resistive heating up to 450°C and excitation frequencies in the 250- to 375-kHz range. Time-domain peak spacing analysis was used to track the oscillation frequencies of individual grating reflections as the temperature varied.The results show clear, repeatable time domain reflections and a decrease in the tracked ultrasonic frequency with increasing temperature. For the uniform frequency grating waveguide, the first grating exhibited an approximately linear response, while subsequent monitored gratings along the waveguide showed departures from linearity. The nonlinearity of subsequent gratings was significantly improved by the multifrequency grating design used in the second waveguide. Linear fits yielded sensitivities ranging from approximately −30 to −57 Hz/°C for the different frequency multipoint gratings.These results demonstrate the feasibility of compact, multipoint waveguide thermometry. Future integration with radiation-tolerant transducers and suitable waveguide materials could support the development of a radiation-resistant UMWTS for fusion divertor diagnostics.

title: Suppressed stiffness of energetic particle transport due to thermal plasma nonlinearity in tokamak plasmas
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Energetic particle (EP) transport stiffness plays a crucial role in determining EP confinement in tokamak plasmas. This work investigates the impact of nonlinear thermal plasma dynamics on EP transport using global gyrokinetic simulations with the TRIMEG code. Simulations are performed for the ITPA toroidal Alfvén eigenmode (TAE) benchmark, and extended to beta-induced Alfvén eigenmodes (BAE) and reversed shear Alfvén eigenmodes (RSAE). Two models are compared: a fully nonlinear treatment of all species and a reduced model with only nonlinear EP. For the TAE simulations, while the linear properties of the instability are identical in both cases, significant differences arise in the nonlinear regime. The inclusion of thermal plasma nonlinearity leads to a reduced saturation level following an overshoot phase and modifies the radial mode structure, including mode broadening and poloidal harmonic splitting. These changes significantly affect EP transport. In particular, the dependence of the EP flux on the EP drive becomes weaker when nonlinear thermal plasma dynamics are included. The saturation level changes from an approximately quadratic scaling to a weaker, nearly linear dependence, leading to a reduced scaling of EP flux with the EP gradient from quartic to quadratic. Zonal flow generation is observed but found to play a minor role in regulating the instability. Without accounting for thermal nonlinearity, the EP flux can be overestimated by an order of magnitude. In addition to the TAE, the BAE and RSAE have also been simulated, demonstrating the similar effects of the thermal plasma nonlinearity on mitigating the saturation level. These results demonstrate that nonlinear thermal plasma effects provide an important feedback mechanism that reduces EP transport stiffness and regulates Alfvénic mode saturation. This feature is therefore essential for predictive modeling of energetic particle confinement in burning plasmas such as ITER.</jats:p>

title: Reconciling chemical models of X-ray Thomson Scattering with the Bethe f -sum rule
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>X-ray Thomson scattering (XRTS) is a key diagnostic for high-energy-density plasmas, which can exhibit significant quantum effects even at elevated temperatures. XRTS experiments are commonly interpreted using the Chihara decomposition, that was derived in the chemical picture and, thus, separates contributions from bound and free electrons. Despite being the de-facto standard for analysing measurements, a well-known shortcoming is that the standard bound-state treatment in the form of the impulse approximation fails to satisfy fundamental theoretical constraints, most notably the Bethe f -sum rule (BFSR). The problem arises due to the usage of plane waves in the impulse approximation as well as non-negligible contributions from bound-bound transitions. In this work, we present an analytical extension of the Chihara decomposition of the dynamic structure factor for matter in the ground state, using hydrogenic bound-free and bound-bound transitions. We demonstrate that compliance with the BFSR is only achieved when bound-bound transitions are explicitly included and an exact treatment of the bound-free contribution is applied. Therefore, the analytic model solves an important issue that has plagued the interpretation of XRTS experiments and represents the ground work for future finite temperature extensions. Finally, detector raytracing simulations for atomic hydrogen demonstrate experimentally detectable deviations from the standard Chihara model. The model will be made available in the open source XRTS library xDAVE</jats:p>

title: Comparative study of damage on tungsten materials irradiated by ELM-like plasma with different energy densities expected in ITER operations
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>During the operation of the tokamak device, the high heat load released by the core plasma instability events severely affects the structure and performance of tungstenbased divertor materials. For the expected Type I ELMs in future long-pulse steadystate fusion devices, the coaxial gun discharge plasma parameters are designed to simulate the characteristics of low-medium energy density. Under constant initial conditions (discharge frequency, gas-prefilled), the total accumulated heat flux is kept constant by varying the energy density and the number of pulses. By combining the plasma-material interaction process, the temperature evolution of tungsten (W) target under different heat loads and its damage effects are comparatively studied. The results show that when the total energy is fixed, the thermal deposition time scale and the instantaneous temperature gradient lead to different types of damage, including roughening, grain loss, blistering, crack networks, and cracking accompanied by melting. Low-energy-density multi-pulse impacts cause slow heat deposition and small temperature gradients, increasing surface roughness via cyclic thermal stress. Highenergy-density impacts involving only a few pulses cause rapid heat deposition and steep temperature gradients, inducing high thermal stresses that lead to blistering and cracking. The energy density of an individual pulse determines the transition from surface to bulk damage. These results suggest that peak heat load control should take priority over cumulative heat flux limitation in the service design of W targets for fusion devices.</jats:p>

title: Age-Dependent Health Risk Assessment of Uranium in Drinking Water from Mining-Affected Regions of Bikaner and the Aravalli Hills of Jhunjhunu District, Rajasthan, India
abstract: Fresh ground water is essential for human consumption and agricultural irrigation however in arid and mining areas the fresh groundwater may be contaminated with uranium. High uranium concentration in drinking water is a big concern due to both the radiological and chemical toxicity potential health risks. The mobility and transport of uranium in groundwater may be affected by mining and local hydrogeologic conditions, hence need for site-specific investigations and in-depth health risk assessments. The present study investigates uranium concentration in groundwater samples collected from various mining-affected areas of Bikaner and Aravalli Hills and Khetri regions of Jhunjhunu districts in northern Rajasthan India. One hundred groundwater samples were collected from 20 different locations at different depths, with five individual samples taken from each location. Uranium concentration was analyzed by LED fluorimeter along with water chemistry—pH, electrical conductance (EC), total dissolved solids (TDS). Health risks were estimated separately using age-dependent annual effective dose (AED) calculations for radiological exposure and lifetime average daily dose (LADD) and hazard quotient (HQ) for chemical toxicity. The results indicate that uranium concentrations vary between 28.1 ± 3 to 172.7 ± 15 µg/L. Nineteen out of twenty location-wise mean concentrations exceed the WHO and USEPA guideline of 30 µg/L and a strong correlation coefficient was observed with groundwater depth (r = 0.866, R2 = 0.7494, p < .001), TDS (r = 0.91, R2 = 0.8302, p < .001) and electrical conductivity (r = 0.86, R2 = 0.7492, p < .001). Infants receive the highest AED doses among all age groups however all doses are below than ICRP reference value of 1 mSv/y. HQ values exceed the WHO, 2026 guidelines of one at all locations while LADD values vary between 0.80 and 4.93 µg/kg·day, indicating potential chemical toxicity risks. Hence groundwater collected from mining-impacted areas has higher concentrations of uranium than drinking-water guideline values indicate greater chemical toxicity health risks than radiological impacts. These findings indicate that 19 out of the 20 location-wise mean concentrations exceed the WHO and USEPA recommend value of 30 µg/L, and eight out of 20 exceeds the AERB prescribed value the 60 µg/L. The estimated radiological doses for all the age groups are below the recommended dose value as given by ICRP, however indicating a higher chemical (nephrotoxic) toxicity risk due to HQ values exceed the WHO, 2026 guidelines of one at all locations. The statistical correlation between the concentration of uranium and groundwater depth, TDS, and electrical conductivity indicates that uranium concentrations may increase with increase these physiochemical parameters. Further hydrochemical characterization, additional seasonal sampling, and uncertainty in exposure assumptions are needed for further work to refine the uranium assessment. Remediation and regular monitoring of drinking-water sources are recommended to reduce the exposure risk in affected locations.

title: Experimental characterization of thin-foil heating by counter-propagating kJ-class ultra-intense laser
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In fast-ignition laser fusion, understanding high-density plasma heating driven by&#xD;picosecond ultra-intense lasers is essential. Thin-foil heating under counter irradiation was&#xD;experimentally characterized using the kilojoule-class picosecond LFEX laser, and the&#xD;associated experimental constraints were clarified. Counter-irradiation was realized via&#xD;plasma-mirror-based beam steering, and a comparison between 90-degree and 180-degree&#xD;reflection configurations showed that the 180-degree configuration enables&#xD;counter-irradiation at intensities exceeding 10$^{18}$ W/cm$^2$.&#xD; Cu and Ti doped deuterated polystyrene thin foil were developed to allow simultaneous measurements of electron&#xD;temperature and fusion reactions. In counter-illumination experiments using planar&#xD;thin-foil targets, Beam-fusion reactions driven by counter-streaming fast ions were&#xD;observed; however, the electron temperature remained around 2 keV, comparable to&#xD;one-sided irradiation. In contrast, one-sided irradiation combining pulse cleaning and&#xD;laser-guiding-cone focusing achieved an electron temperature of 10 keV. These results&#xD;indicate that, at intensities on the order of 10$^{18}$ W/cm$^2$, high contrast and enhanced&#xD;focusing are required for effective plasma heating.</jats:p>

title: Edge ion heat flux as a key parameter of the L-H transition: insights from ion and electron heating experiments on TCV
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We investigate the role of the edge ion heat flux $Q_\mathrm{i,edge}$ in the L--H transition on TCV, comparing purely electron-heated (ECRH) and dominantly ion-heated (low-energy NBI) plasmas. The two heating schemes produce different $P_\mathrm{L-H}$ trends. ECRH discharges exhibit the characteristic non-monotonic density dependence, while NBI discharges show a monotonically increasing power threshold with &#xD;values up to three times lower at comparable densities. However, when expressed in terms of the edge ion heat flux, both datasets show a monotonic density dependence even at low density, where the electron--ion collisional energy exchange is inefficient, suggesting that the ion heat flux, not the total loss power, plays a key role in the physics of the L--H transition. These results extend the critical edge ion heat flux criterion to a carbon-wall device and to dominantly ion-heated conditions, and support $Q_\mathrm{i,edge}$-based approaches as a physics-grounded complement to conventional $P_\mathrm{L-H}$ scalings.</jats:p>

title: Core-edge integrated scenario with a high-performance hybrid core, naturally small ELMs, and a dissipative divertor on DIII-D
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Operating at higher gas fueling and lower injected torque has improved the core-edge integration and reactor relevance of the hybrid scenario. Progress was made in the core, pedestal and edge of the plasma. In the core, higher density ($>50\%$ increase compared to past hybrid plasmas) lowered the heat diffusivity and turbulent energy flux. In particular, electron cyclotron heating (ECH) had less of a deleterious effect on confinement at higher density. High fueling rates led to an increase in separatrix density, which destabilizes a higher n ($n>50$) resistive-ballooning mode at the foot of the pedestal. This higher n mode is associated with smaller, higher frequency edge localized modes (ELMs) ($f_{ELM} \geq 500$ Hz) that limit pedestal growth below the peeling-ballooning stability limit associated with type-I ELMs. Access to this small-ELM regime requires both a wide density pedestal (from higher gas puffing) and sufficiently high plasma squareness. These higher frequency ELMs have oscillations in the stored energy of $<1\%$ with each ELM and lower peak heat flux to the divertor compared to type-I ELMs. The higher edge density with a wider density pedestal also helps to maintain core performance through partial divertor detachment. Puffing N$_2$ gas from the private flux region of the divertor led to partial detachment without a decrease in $\beta_N$, while maintaining pedestal temperatures of $\sim1$~keV. Under the assumption of a hybrid-like pedestal, FASTRAN projections of the high-density hybrid scenario to a compact fusion pilot plant produce positive net electric power.</jats:p>

title: Characterization of a novel disruption mechanism during plasma current ramp-down in the ADITYA-U tokamak
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Safe termination of a tokamak plasma discharge remains a challenge due to the high risk of encountering a magnetohydrodynamic (MHD)-driven disruption during controlled ramp-down of the plasma current. During the current ramp-down phase of ADITYA-U discharges, the occurrence of MHD-driven disruptions cannot be described by the conventional locked-mode disruption (LMD) mechanism. Analysing hundreds of ADITYA-U discharges, it has been observed that when some specific plasma parameters exceeds a threshold rate, the disruption is always preceded by a steady rise in MHD mode-rotation frequency, followed by a sudden cessation of mode-rotation frequency before the current quench. Moreover, it has been found that the occurrence of this type of disruption depends mainly on the current decay rate and magnitude and the edge safety factor (qedge). Although the disruption seems to be predominantly governed only by the m/n=2/1 drift–tearing modes, the precursor phase in this kind of disruption survives for relatively much shorter times as compared to the conventional locked mode disruptions. Further investigation revealed that during the plasma current decay phase, the core radiation increases significantly, indicating a hollow temperature profile. This leads to destabilization of the MHD mode, which seems to be primarily responsible for the plasma disruption.</jats:p>

title: Neutron Irradiation in Thermoelectrics for Space Nuclear Power: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Thermoelectric generators are critical solid-state energy converters in space nuclear power systems, where their long-term operational stability under neutron irradiation critically determines mission lifetime.This review presents a systematic overview of neutron irradiation effects on established thermoelectric materials (e.g., Bi 2 Te 3 , PbTe, SiGe) and emerging candidates (e.g., half-Heuslers, skutterudites, Zintl phases). We systematically analyze experimental data on the evolution of electrical conductivity, Seebeck coefficient, and thermal conductivity, revealing the complex interplay among neutron fluence, energy spectrum, and irradiation temperature. Building upon empirical trends, we develop a multi-scale framework linking microscopic damage events to macroscopic degradation of thermoelectric transport properties. We further evaluate the efficacy of post-irradiation recovery strategies, including annealing and in situ thermal recovery. Finally, we identify critical pathways for future research, emphasizing the rational design of irradiation-tolerant materials via microstructural engineering and composition optimization, the development of predictive models coupling defect dynamics to performance, and the advancement of in situ characterization techniques for extreme environments. This review aims to establish a foundational knowledge base and a strategic roadmap for advancing high-reliability thermoelectrics toward next-generation space explorations and terrestrial nuclear energy applications.

title: Modeling the Separation of Silicon Isotopes in Square Cascades: Impact of Material Losses and Light Gas Production
abstract: This study investigates isotopic separation and concentration distributions within a square cascade to assess the effects of material losses and light HF gas generation. A computational model was developed for this analysis, focusing on four key parameters in cascades with 50 and 25 stages: stage feed rate, P/F ratio, cascade feed, and unit separation factor, specifically for the SiF4 isotope mixture. The results reveal that the cascade feed rate, stage feed rate, and P/F ratio significantly influence the HF concentration in the light product at the final stage, particularly under conditions of high material losses. Notably, all HF gas is directed towards the end of the cascade, leading to a sudden increase in concentration in the light product at the final stage. Furthermore, the extent of material losses and the accumulation of HF gas in the last stage increase with the number of stages in the cascade. As the material loss coefficient rises, the isotopic separation of the target isotope in longer cascades diminishes compared to shorter ones. Additionally, increased material losses result in a reduced depletion of the light isotope at the end of the heavy product, contributing to a greater overall loss of the target isotope.

title: Physics-informed neural surrogates for joint spent-fuel decay heat and pool thermal screening
authors: Bruno Rucy Carneiro Alves de Lima
abstract: • Includes a 20,000-case spent-fuel decay heat and pool thermal response benchmark. • Physics-informed networks penalize thermal and decay-heat inconsistencies. • Joint in-distribution normalized error is 52.2 % below the standard neural ensemble. • The selected model reaches 9.25 % mean absolute percentage error on calorimetry. Rapid spent fuel pool (SFP) assessment requires fast, reliable estimates of decay heat and thermal response across heterogeneous fuel inventories and degraded cooling states. This study establishes a new, reproducible benchmark by sampling three-cohort pressurized water reactor spent-fuel inventories, deriving decay heat from an open Serpent2 depletion library, and propagating the resulting heat load through a reduced-order subcooled pool energy balance. The proposed physics-informed neural network (PINN) embeds heat-balance consistency, physically correct transient direction, and decay-heat monotonicity into supervised learning. These constraints directly couple the heat-load and temperature targets and discourage physically inconsistent predictions under domain shift. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first openly reproducible study to evaluate a problem-specific PINN for joint SFP decay-heat and bulk-temperature prediction using independent calorimetry and explicit domain-shift tests. The latter is compared on independent and identically distributed (IID) and domain-shift conditions with engineering and statistical baselines, multilayer perceptron (MLP) ensembles, physics-feature MLPs and decay-heat residual hybrids. Architectures and hyperparameters are selected using validation scores; performance is assessed through repeated holdouts and external CLAB calorimetry. Direct Serpent interpolation achieves 5.65 % MAPE on 16 measured 17 × 17 CLAB assemblies, reduced to 1.73 % by the reported 27.1 W bias correction. Across five random seeds, the selected PINN MLP attains an IID mean normalized RMSE of 0.031, reducing IID mean normalized RMSE by 52.2 % relative to the standard MLP ensemble, while achieving 9.25 % external decay-heat MAPE. The results demonstrate that problem-specific physics constraints materially improve rapid, simultaneous heat-load and thermal-response prediction.

title: Development of a one-dimensional thermal–hydraulics framework for nuclear reactor analysis in OpenFOAM
abstract: Modern nuclear reactor safety analyses increasingly rely on multi-fidelity approaches, combining high-resolution CFD and porous-medium models in localized regions with lower-fidelity system thermal–hydraulic models for full-plant simulations. Within this hierarchy, one-dimensional system codes are essential, capturing entire reactor circuits at a fraction of the cost of higher-fidelity methods. In this context, the foamForNuclear platform has recently been developed as an OpenFOAM-based multi-physics, multi-fidelity framework enabling the coupling of porous-medium and CFD regions within a unified environment. However, it lacks a native 1D thermal–hydraulic capability and therefore depends on external system codes for plant-scale analyses, limiting full integration within the OpenFOAM ecosystem. This work presents a new OpenFOAM-native 1D thermal–hydraulic framework fully integrated into FFN. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first such implementation embedded directly within OpenFOAM and designed for consistent coupling with higher-fidelity models. The formulation is based on 1D conservation equations for mass, momentum, and energy, representing pipes, junctions, pumps, and hydraulic discontinuities, and is currently restricted to single-phase flow. Component-level verification against analytical solutions shows very good agreement for hydraulic and thermal test cases. System-level performance is assessed using a representative reactor-circuit transient and compared against the system code TRACE, showing good agreement in pressure, flow redistribution, and temperature evolution. This work establishes a consistent foundation for OpenFOAM-native system thermal–hydraulics within FFN and enables future extensions to advanced multi-physics applications, including two-phase flow modelling.

title: Tangential gas injection-enhanced fuel elements for centrifugal nuclear thermal rockets: A thermal-hydraulic analysis
abstract: This study proposes the application of tangential hydrogen injection as an alternative swirl-generation concept for centrifugal nuclear thermal rocket (CNTR) fuel elements and numerically evaluates its gas-side thermal-hydraulic performance. Two swirl-generation mechanisms are investigated: tangential inlet-induced (TII) swirl, produced by tangential hydrogen injection, and wall rotation-induced (WRI) swirl, produced by mechanically rotating boundaries. A two-dimensional axisymmetric-swirl unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (URANS) framework with Reynolds Stress Model (RSM) turbulence closure was validated against experimental swirling-flow data and subsequently applied to compare the two configurations under matched swirl intensity, inlet mass flow rate, geometry, and thermal boundary conditions. The results show fundamentally different radial swirl distributions: TII produces a Rankine-vortex-type flow with swirl concentrated toward the core and decaying downstream, whereas WRI maintains a forced-vortex-type flow with strong near-wall tangential motion. At the baseline condition of 200 RPM-equivalent swirl and a wall heat flux of 3000 W/m 2 , TII increases the global Nusselt number from 10.63 to 12.66, corresponding to an approximately 19% enhancement over WRI, while producing nearly identical pressure loss. Increasing the imposed swirl from 100 to 600 RPM-equivalent increases the global Nusselt number of TII from 11.50 to 16.48, whereas that of WRI remains nearly unchanged. The resulting Figure of Merit (FoM) for TII increases from approximately 1.06 to 1.63. The radial pressure differences generated by TII and WRI are comparable near the injection region, indicating that both mechanisms generate centrifugal fields that may contribute to fuel retention; however, the TII-induced field decays downstream while the WRI field is continuously sustained by wall rotation. Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of TII for enhancing gas-side heat transfer while generating a centrifugal field and potentially reducing reliance on mechanically rotating components in CNTR fuel elements. Further, two-phase simulations, injector-geometry and outlet-orifice optimization, and system-level analyses are required to determine its feasibility under representative CNTR operating conditions.
